title: Why are we saying 'Caesar' wrong? | TITLES & POWER

entries.note: Default title for any supreme leader; spelled cyning in Old English for any ruler or sovereign, and related to [[same-root:kin]], kings representing a kinship.
Related to [[same-root:king]], since kings originally represented a kinship.
Its -dom is not related to [[unrelated:dominion]] or [[unrelated:dominate]] but to [[from:doom]], so it is a king's judgment rather than his dominion.
Looks like the source of the -dom in [[unrelated:kingdom]] but isn't.
Looks like the source of the -dom in [[unrelated:kingdom]] but isn't.
In Old English meant a law, statute, decree or judgment upon you; it gave the -dom of [[gave:kingdom]], and a judge was a [[see:doomsman]].
Old English word for a judge, built on [[from:doom]] in its sense of judgment.
German cognate of [[same-root:king]], whose feminine form is [[gave:Königin]].
Old English cwēn, a poetic word for a [[see:wife]], from the same root as Greek [[same-root:gyne]]; came to mean ruler because queens were kings' wives.
In Old English meant a woman, not necessarily a married one; it became part of [[gave:woman]].
Developed from Old English [[from:wifman]].
Greek for woman, from the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:queen]], used in words like [[gave:gynecology]].
Uses Greek [[from:gyne]], woman.
Latin for king, with the feminised [[see:regina]]; related to Sanskrit [[same-root:raja]].
Latin for queen, a feminised form of [[see:rex]], more logical than English [[see:queen]].
German for queen, simply the feminine of [[from:König]], unlike English [[see:queen]].
The most famous English monarch with a moniker, also known as William the Bastard before his conquests.
Unready means ill-advised, from an Old English verb to advise; a pun, since Æthelred, from [[from:æthel]], can mean well advised.
Element starting Old English kings' names, meaning noble or great; different from the athel- of [[see:ætheling]], though both may be spelled with [[see:ash]].
A pious king made a saint, perhaps named for confessing fanatically; the name may evoke the earlier sense of [[see:confess]].
Originally meant to avow or declare rather than to admit something, as discussed in an earlier episode.
Son of [[see:William the Conqueror]], called Rufus, red, for his red beard or hair.
King John, the youngest legitimate son, was bequeathed very little land and so called Lackland.
Edward I, so tall he was called Longshanks, shanks being the lower legs; the epithet also appears in Lord of the Rings.
Lothbrok, meaning woolly trousers, sounds like a surname but is an epithet; father of [[see:Ivar the Boneless]].
A Spanish ruler said to foam at the mouth when upset, probably a popular rather than official nickname.
A ruler from the same Spanish region as [[see:Alfonso the Slobberer]], so called because he had gout.
Another ruler known by a memorable epithet.
Son of [[see:Ragnar Lothbrok]], perhaps named for a problem with his legs that stopped him walking; he ended up living in Derbyshire.
Means first, a chief leader, from Latin [[from:princeps]] and related to [[same-root:prime]]; brought by the Normans, before whom [[see:ætheling]] was used.
Related to [[same-root:prince]]; the prime of [[see:prime minister]] shares a root with [[same-root:premier]].
Anglo-Saxon word used before the Normans brought [[see:prince]]; athel- refers to a noble family and -ing to a member, usually a young man.
Name of the plant kingsfoil in Lord of the Rings, a nod to [[see:ætheling]].
Old English letter æ, a cross between a and e, which makes [[see:æthel]] and the athel- of [[see:ætheling]] look almost identical.
Old Germanic title of Old Norse origin that survived the Normans, who would usually have said count; related to Viking [[same-root:jarl]]s.
Norman title England never adopted; from Latin co-, with, plus ire, to go, a Roman title for a provincial governor or attendant; Rob calls it a [[see:companion]].
Viking title related to [[same-root:earl]].
From Old English ealdorman, the Anglo-Saxon counterpart of Norse-origin [[see:earl]]; now a local judicial post, it is the same word as elderman.
The verb comes from French conter, from the same root as [[same-root:compute]]; it shares a prefix but not a root with the noble title.
Shares its root verb with the verb to count.
The Sesame Street character, who on etymological grounds needn't count anything at all.
Means someone you eat bread with, leading from the count to other bread people like the [[see:lord]].
From Old English [[from:hlāford]], meaning loaf guardian or loaf ward.
A further extension of the bread theme of [[see:lord]], originally meaning bread kneader.
Apparently a separate household title for someone who consumed bread rather than providing it like the [[see:lord]].
Scottish interpretation of [[from:lord]], still found as a title today.
Anglo-Saxon title that began meaning follower or attendant and became a leadership title; [[see:Macbeth]] becomes thane of Cawdor.
The best-known [[see:thane]], who becomes thane of Cawdor.
Originally a servant, as German [[same-root:Knecht]] still means, later servants of the king; never replaced by [[see:cavalier]]s.
German word for a servant, related to [[same-root:knight]].
Never displaced [[see:knight]]; English Cavaliers were a much later deliberate import.
Brought over by the Normans, from a Latin word that simply means a man.
Jokingly glossed as a lady man, from [[from:baron]].
From Latin [[from:dux]], leader, related to [[same-root:conduct]], [[same-root:educate]], [[same-root:induce]] and [[same-root:produce]].
Related to [[same-root:duke]].
Related to [[same-root:duke]].
Related to [[same-root:duke]].
Related to [[same-root:duke]].
With empress, from Latin [[from:imperator]], from imperare, to command; first a military title, it became a permanent honorific from [[see:Julius Caesar]] onward.
Gaius Julius Caesar, from whom Imperator became a permanent honorific and after whom all later [[see:Caesar]]s are named.
A hereditary [[see:cognomen]]; its meaning is uncertain (thick hair, grey eyes, cutting); Romans pronounced the C as K, as in [[gave:Kaiser]].
The third element of a Roman citizen's name, originally a family name that became hereditary, like [[see:Caesar]].
Augustus Caesar, after [[see:Julius Caesar]], from whom rulers were called [[see:Caesar]]s.
Fits the probably inaccurate theory that [[see:Caesar]] is related to cutting.
Also from a Latin verb meaning to cut into pieces, as in [[see:caesarean section]].
German form of [[from:Caesar]], keeping the Roman K sound.
Spelled tsar or czar, a rendering of [[from:Caesar]] or [[from:Kaiser]].
Means great house: first the Egyptian king's palace, then the king himself, like [[see:White House]] for the US executive, a [[see:metonymy]].
Used as a stand-in for the US executive branch, like [[see:pharaoh]] for the king.
Any stand-in for another thing, as in [[see:pharaoh]], with [[see:synecdoche]] as one form; it came up in their nym episode.
A part standing for a whole, such as a roof for a house or a suit for a businessperson; a form of [[see:metonymy]].
Roman title that survives today, meaning old man, an elder leader.
Persian title meaning king, sometimes grouped with [[see:tsar]], [[see:Kaiser]] and [[see:Caesar]] but much older.
Title of Sunni Muslim leaders meaning successor; disagreement over who succeeded Muhammad as first caliph split [[see:Sunni]] and [[see:Shia]] Islam.
Branch of Islam that split from [[see:Shia]] over who the first [[see:caliph]] was.
Branch of Islam that split from [[see:Sunni]] over who the first [[see:caliph]] was.
Most associated with the Ottoman Empire, simply meaning a king or ruler; his wife is a [[see:sultana]].
A sultan's wife and a dried seedless white grape, named possessively after the [[see:sultan]], perhaps one fleeing a tiger, more likely for grapes from Izmir.
The smallest dried grapes, made from red grapes, smaller than [[see:sultana]]s and [[see:raisins]].
The biggest dried grapes, made from white grapes that still have their seeds, unlike [[see:sultana]]s.
Indian title meaning king, from Sanskrit, related to [[same-root:rex]] and Irish [[same-root:rí]] through a root meaning to move in a straight line.
Irish title for king, related to [[same-root:raja]].
Related to [[same-root:raja]].
Said to be related to [[same-root:raja]].
Related to [[same-root:raja]].
Said to be related to [[same-root:raja]].
Related to [[same-root:raja]].
Related to [[same-root:raja]] through the idea of going in a straight line.
Both senses, measuring stick and leader, are related to [[same-root:raja]].
Means emperor, so the leader of the Inca was himself called the Inca, or the [[see:Sapa Inca]].
Title of the Inca leader, meaning the only emperor.
Title of the Aztec leader, huey meaning great, above the [[see:tlatoani]].
Aztec rulers in the stratum beneath the [[see:huey tlatoani]]; the word means speaker, which sounds very modern.
Noble title beneath the [[see:tlatoani]], named after a deity, sharing its serpent element with [[same-root:Quetzalcoatl]].
Feathered serpent god of wind, wisdom and learning; a dinosaur named after him came up in their dinosaur episode.
Religious or administrative, means one who serves or attends, a lesser one, related to [[same-root:minus]] and [[same-root:minor]].
Slightly oxymoronic first lesser one, yet accurate for the most senior elected politician; possibly first used pejoratively; its prime relates to [[same-root:premier]].
Related to [[same-root:minister]].
Related to [[same-root:minister]].
Another political leader's title, sharing a root with the [[same-root:prime]] of [[see:prime minister]].
Someone who presides, from the 14th century; later for governors and college heads, used at Jamestown in 1608, then for the Continental Congress and the US chief executive.
Among those styled president of the council at Jamestown, the first use of [[see:president]] in what is now the US.
From Latin inaugurare, to take omens from birds' flight or install someone when omens were favourable; based on the [[from:augur]].
Roman religious official who read omens, mainly bird behaviour, to judge the gods' views; possibly related to [[from?:avis]], bird; things still don't augur well.
Joe Biden's dog, whose ceremony prompted the headline pun [[see:indoguration]].
Headline pun on [[see:inauguration]] for an event for Biden's dog [[see:Major]]; Rob notes it doesn't work in a British accent.
Means doorkeeper; in the late Roman Empire the role grew into clerical and notary duties, then gained importance in England, recorded in 1123.
Today's title of the British finance minister, from [[from:chancellor]].
Rule by the people, the demos, whose root may mean city; in [[see:Plato]]'s scheme it follows [[see:oligarchy]] and degenerates into [[see:tyranny]].
Listed five forms of government, each degenerating into the next, with [[see:aristocracy]] as the best.
Rule by the best, which [[see:Plato]] thought the best system, degenerating into [[see:timocracy]].
Rule by honour or worth: for [[see:Plato]] those motivated by honour, for [[see:Aristotle]] property owners; it degenerates into [[see:oligarchy]].
Interpreted [[see:timocracy]] as rule by people with property.
Rule by the few, olig- meaning few; in [[see:Plato]]'s scheme it degenerates into [[see:democracy]].
Having few syllables, ironically a mouthful, making it a [[see:heterological]] word.
Describes a word that doesn't describe itself, like [[see:oligosyllabic]] and [[see:monosyllabic]].
Another [[see:heterological]] word.
What [[see:democracy]] degenerates into in [[see:Plato]]'s scheme: rule by a [[see:tyrant]].
Someone who seizes power without the legal right to it.
Rule by God, in practice by the church as God's representatives; some still exist.
Rule by the wealthy.
Rule by one's own authority; Byzantine rulers styled themselves autocrats to show independence from senate and pope; [[see:John Milton]] dismissed [[see:monarchy]] as one.
Dismissed [[see:monarchy]] as an [[see:autocracy]].
Means strength or might, from Greek [[from:kratos]]; an -ocrat participates in one; implies more might than [[see:-archy]].
Power by means of power, rule by strength or might, from the same root as [[same-root:-ocracy]].
Means rule or leadership, implying rule more than the might of [[see:-ocracy]].
Rule of one, with the [[see:-archy]] ending; compare [[see:monocracy]].
Presumably means the same as [[see:monarchy]], rule of one.
Rule by the worst in society, from Greek [[from:kakistos]]; a word of the year last year according to several sources.
Rule of the seas, applied to ancient maritime powers; Jess misheard it as [[see:phallocracy]].
Rule by men, which Rob says describes most of the world's governments; also called [[see:androcracy]].
Rule by men, like [[see:phallocracy]]; its opposite is [[see:gynocracy]].
Rule by women, the opposite of [[see:androcracy]], sometimes called [[see:pornocracy]].
Name given to the influence of [[see:Theodora]] and her daughter [[see:Marozia]] over Rome and the papacy, as their lovers and sons became popes.
10th-century [[see:senatrix]] called a shameless harlot who ruled like a man; her rule with [[see:Marozia]] was called a [[see:pornocracy]].
Daughter of [[see:Theodora]], sharing her influence over Rome and the papacy in the [[see:pornocracy]].
Means producing ducks, from their Samuel Johnson episode; it prompts the joke [[see:anatocracy]].
Joke coinage for rule by ducks, inspired by [[see:anatiferous]].
A female senator, new to Rob; also senatress, but -trix, matching the male -or, is the properly Latin ending.
Rule by elders or the old.
Rule by thieves, or stolen rule.
Rule by an army or the military.
Sacred or priestly rule, from Greek [[from:hieros]], sacred.
Universal rule, from pan-; Jess is puzzled by the T, though Rob notes plain panarchy sounds related to pants.
Rule by all equals, a coinage by [[see:Samuel Taylor Coleridge]] and [[see:Robert Southey]] for a utopian society.
Coined [[see:pantisocracy]] with [[see:Robert Southey]].
Coined [[see:pantisocracy]] with [[see:Samuel Taylor Coleridge]].
The delegation of power to the wise or smart.
Rule by workers.
Mob rule, dating from the 1700s rather than recently; [[see:ochlocracy]] is a more technical-sounding alternative.
More technical-sounding alternative to [[see:mobocracy]], meaning rule by the mob or masses.
A modern coinage from ad hoc.
Not one of the original Greek forms; rule by desks, from French [[from:bureau]], a desk or wardrobe, meaning rule from an office.
Another of the forms of government named in the list of -ocracies.
Germanic ending for a condition of being that can denote a government when attached to a ruler, as in [[see:dictatorship]] and [[see:cyningscipe]].
An example of a form of rule ending in [[see:-ship]].
Old English word for kingship, an example of [[see:-ship]].
Old English word for knighthood, an example of [[see:-ship]].
Meaning friendhood, an example of [[see:-ship]].
Old word for enmity, discussed in an earlier episode, another example of [[see:-ship]].
